facts: The Arctic Tern has the longest migration of any bird, traveling roughly 44,000 miles (71,000 km) each year from Arctic to Antarctic and back.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They can also hover in place by flapping their wings up to 80 times per second!
A group of crows is called a 'murder', while a group of owls is called a 'parliament'. Ravens gather in an 'unkindness' or 'conspiracy'.
The Peregrine Falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, reaching speeds over 240 mph (386 km/h) during its hunting dive.
Penguins propose to their mates by giving them a pebble. If the female accepts, she places it in her nest.
Albatrosses can fly for hours without flapping their wings, and some species can circumnavigate the globe in just 46 days.
A woodpecker's tongue wraps around its skull to protect its brain from the impact of pecking, which can occur 20 times per second.
The Bar-tailed Godwit holds the record for longest non-stop flight, traveling 7,500 miles from Alaska to New Zealand without rest.
Owls cannot move their eyes in their sockets. Instead, they can rotate their heads up to 270 degrees.
The lyrebird of Australia can mimic almost any sound it hears, including chainsaws, car alarms, and camera shutters.
Flamingos are born grey and white. They turn pink from eating algae and shrimp that contain carotenoid pigments.
Ravens are among the smartest birds and can solve complex puzzles, plan for the future, and even hold 'grudges'.
The smallest bird in the world is the Bee Hummingbird, weighing less than a penny at just 2 grams.
Crows can recognize individual human faces and hold grudges for years. They can even teach other crows about dangerous humans.
Emperor Penguins can dive over 1,800 feet deep and hold their breath for more than 20 minutes while hunting.
The Hoatzin, also called the 'stinkbird', has a unique digestive system similar to cows and smells like manure.
Chickens can recognize and remember over 100 different faces, including humans and other chickens.
The Common Swift can stay airborne for 10 months straight, sleeping, eating, and even mating while flying.
A single hummingbird visits between 1,000 and 2,000 flowers per day for nectar.
Vultures have extremely acidic stomach acid (pH close to 0) that allows them to safely digest rotting meat and neutralize harmful bacteria.
The Kakapo, a flightless parrot from New Zealand, is the world's heaviest parrot and can live over 90 years.
Male Emperor Penguins endure Antarctic winter without eating for up to 4 months while incubating their eggs.
The Clark's Nutcracker can remember the locations of up to 30,000 seeds it has buried, even months later under snow.
Ostriches have the largest eyes of any land animal, measuring nearly 2 inches in diameter—bigger than their brain!
The Red-billed Quelea is the most abundant wild bird species on Earth, with an estimated population of 1.5 billion.
Cassowaries are considered the world's most dangerous bird. Their powerful legs and dagger-like claws can be lethal.
Pigeons can detect earthquakes and magnetic fields, helping them navigate. They were used to carry messages in both World Wars.
The Shoebill stork can stand motionless for hours waiting for prey and has one of the most powerful beaks in the bird kingdom.
Barn Owls can locate prey in complete darkness using only sound. Their hearing is asymmetric to help pinpoint exact locations.
Male Greater Sage-Grouse perform elaborate courtship displays, inflating air sacs and making popping sounds to attract females.
The Wandering Albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, stretching up to 11.5 feet (3.5 meters).
Magpies are one of the few non-mammal species that can recognize themselves in a mirror.
The Sword-billed Hummingbird has a bill longer than its entire body (excluding tail), specially adapted for deep flowers.
Australian Magpies can learn to mimic human speech and other complex sounds.
Kiwis have nostrils at the end of their beaks (unique among birds) and hunt by smell rather than sight.
A peacock's elaborate tail feathers can contain over 200 individual 'eye' patterns and are shed annually.
The African Grey Parrot has the intelligence of a 5-year-old child and can learn over 1,000 words.
Swifts mate in the air while flying. The entire copulation happens mid-flight in just a few seconds.
Secretary Birds stamp on snakes with a force 5 times their body weight to kill them.
Blue Jays can imitate the calls of hawks to scare other birds away from food sources.
The Great Hornbill's casque (helmet on head) is hollow and acts as a resonating chamber to amplify its calls.
Puffins can hold multiple fish (up to 60!) in their beaks at once thanks to backward-pointing spines on their tongue and palate.
Hummingbirds have the highest metabolism of all animals—their heart can beat over 1,200 times per minute.
The Elf Owl, smallest owl in the world, is only about 5-6 inches tall and weighs around 1.4 ounces.
Golden Eagles can spot a rabbit from over 2 miles away thanks to their exceptional eyesight.
Some species of parrots mate for life and show signs of mourning when their partner dies.
The Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture) drops bones from great heights to crack them open and access the marrow inside.
Sandhill Cranes have been around for over 10 million years, making them one of the oldest living bird species.
A duck's quack doesn't echo, and scientists still debate why this phenomenon occurs.
The Great Blue Heron can strike at prey in 1/100th of a second, faster than you can blink.
Turkey Vultures can smell carrion from over a mile away, one of the few birds with a highly developed sense of smell.
The Resplendent Quetzal was considered divine by ancient Aztec and Maya civilizations and was more valuable than gold.
Kookaburras are known as the 'laughing bird' and their call is used to establish territory, often heard at dawn and dusk.
The Alpine Chough holds the record for highest altitude bird nest, breeding at over 21,000 feet in the Himalayas.
Bald Eagles aren't actually bald—their white head feathers make them appear so. The name comes from 'piebald' meaning white-headed.
The Victoria Crowned Pigeon is the largest pigeon species in the world, about the size of a turkey.
Northern Cardinals are one of the few bird species where females also sing, often while sitting on the nest.
Road Runners can run up to 26 mph and prefer running to flying. They're also one of the few animals that eat rattlesnakes.
The Tufted Puffin can dive up to 200 feet underwater and uses its wings to 'fly' through the water.
Barn Swallows can travel up to 600 miles in a single day during migration.
The Hooded Pitohui of New Guinea is one of the only known poisonous birds, with toxins in its skin and feathers.
Superb Fairy-wrens teach their chicks a unique 'password' call while they're still in the egg to identify them later.
The Common Loon's eerie call has been used in countless movies to create an atmospheric wilderness sound.
Male Bowerbirds build elaborate structures decorated with colorful objects to attract females—some even arrange items by color.
The Greater Roadrunner kills rattlesnakes by grabbing them and repeatedly slamming them against rocks.
Andean Condors can fly for up to 100 miles without flapping their wings once, using thermal air currents.
Baby Hoatzins have claws on their wings that help them climb trees, a trait they lose as adults.
The Black Skimmer has a unique lower mandible that's longer than the upper, which it drags through water to catch fish.
Malleefowl don't incubate their eggs with body heat—they bury them in mounds and regulate temperature by adding or removing sand.
The Jacana bird has extremely long toes that distribute its weight, allowing it to walk on lily pads.
Ptarmigans change the color of their feathers with the seasons—brown in summer, white in winter for camouflage.
The Rifleman bird of New Zealand weighs less than 7 grams, making it one of the smallest birds in the world.
Great Crested Grebes perform an elaborate synchronized courtship dance that includes offering each other aquatic plants.
The Palm Cockatoo uses sticks to drum on hollow trees, one of the few examples of musical tool use in nature.
Cedar Waxwings sometimes eat so many fermented berries they become intoxicated and fly erratically.
The Eurasian Jay can mimic the sounds of other animals and has been known to imitate human speech.
Black Vultures mate for life and will attack other vultures that approach their partner.
The Cactus Wren builds multiple nests—one for raising chicks and others for roosting.
White-throated Dippers can walk underwater on the bottom of streams to catch aquatic insects.
The Marvelous Spatuletail hummingbird has only four tail feathers, two of which are elongated with violet disc-shaped tips.
Bohemian Waxwings have been observed getting drunk from fermented rowan berries and crashing into windows.
The Philippine Eagle is one of the largest eagles in the world and can hunt monkeys in the forest canopy.
Rock Pigeons can detect magnetic fields and use the Earth's magnetic field for navigation.
The Potoo bird's camouflage is so effective it looks like a broken tree branch when it's sitting still.
European Starlings were introduced to North America by a group wanting to bring all birds mentioned by Shakespeare to the US.
The Tailorbird literally sews leaves together to create a cup-shaped nest using plant fibers as thread.
Snow Geese migrate in massive flocks that can number in the hundreds of thousands.
The Crested Auklet emits a tangerine-like scent during breeding season, unique among birds.
Scarlet Macaws eat clay from riverbanks to neutralize toxins in the unripe fruits they consume.
The Marabou Stork is sometimes called the 'undertaker bird' due to its hunched posture and black-and-white appearance.
Anna's Hummingbird can survive cold nights by entering a hibernation-like state called torpor, lowering their metabolism by 95%.
The Pied-billed Grebe can control its buoyancy and slowly sink beneath the water surface to hide from predators.
Eurasian Hoopoes have a gland that produces foul-smelling liquid they use to defend their nests from predators.
The Great Spotted Woodpecker can peck up to 20 times per second without getting a headache.
Red Knots migrate from the Arctic to the southern tip of South America, one of the longest migrations of any shorebird.
The Helmeted Hornbill has a solid casque made of keratin that makes up 10% of its body weight.
Budgerigars in the wild are always green and yellow—blue and other colors only exist in captive-bred birds.
The Limpkin's call sounds like a person screaming, earning it the nickname 'crying bird'.
Dippers have a third eyelid that acts like goggles when they're underwater.
The Red Crossbill's crossed bill tips are perfectly adapted for extracting seeds from conifer cones.
Black Swans were thought to be impossible until Dutch explorers discovered them in Australia in the 1600s.
The Greater Honeyguide bird leads honey badgers and humans to beehives, then feeds on the wax after the nest is opened.
Violet Sabrewing hummingbirds have been observed using leaves as roofs over their nests during rain.
The Snowy Owl can detect prey under up to a foot of snow using its exceptional hearing.
Painted Buntings are sometimes called the most beautiful bird in North America due to their vibrant rainbow plumage.
The Southern Ground Hornbill has been known to live over 70 years, making it one of the longest-lived birds.
Turkey Vultures urinate on their own legs to cool down in hot weather, a process called urohidrosis.
The Long-tailed Tit family stays together and helps raise the next generation of chicks.
Hooded Mergansers have a special membrane that protects their eyes underwater while they hunt for fish.
The Bearded Reedling, despite its name, is not actually a tit but is in its own unique family.
Wood Ducks nest in tree cavities up to 65 feet high, and ducklings jump to the ground within 24 hours of hatching.
The Rhinoceros Hornbill's casque is hollow and amplifies its loud calls across the rainforest.
European Bee-eaters can catch and eat up to 250 bees per day, first removing the stinger by beating it against a branch.
The Toco Toucan's large bill helps it regulate body temperature by adjusting blood flow.
Adelie Penguins can leap up to 9 feet out of the water onto ice shelves.
The Harpy Eagle has talons the size of grizzly bear claws and can carry prey weighing half its body weight.
Northern Mockingbirds can learn up to 200 different songs during their lifetime.
The Indian Peafowl's train of feathers can be over 5 feet long and contains around 200 feathers.
Clark's Grebes perform a spectacular 'rushing ceremony' where pairs run across water together during courtship.
The Fiery-throated Hummingbird lives only in the highlands of Costa Rica and Panama.
Great Frigatebirds stay airborne for months at a time, sleeping in 10-second bursts while gliding.
The Rhinoceros Auklet grows a horn-like structure on its bill during breeding season.
Yellow-headed Blackbirds have one of the most distinctive calls of any North American bird.
The Greater Flamingo can filter-feed on microscopic organisms while standing in caustic alkaline lakes.
Acorn Woodpeckers live in family groups and create 'granaries'—trees with thousands of holes, each storing a single acorn.
The Black-capped Chickadee can remember thousands of hiding places where it stores seeds.
Paradise Tanagers have seven different colors on their plumage, making them one of the most colorful birds.
The Magnificent Frigatebird has the largest wingspan-to-body-weight ratio of any bird.
Tree Swallows form enormous flocks during migration that can look like smoke clouds in the sky.
The Superb Lyrebird's tail feathers can take up to 7 years to fully develop.
Red-headed Woodpeckers are one of the few woodpeckers that store food, hiding insects in tree bark crevices.
The Black-browed Albatross can live over 70 years and often returns to the same nesting site for decades.
American Woodcocks have eyes set far back on their heads, giving them 360-degree vision to watch for predators.
The Gouldian Finch comes in three natural color variations: red-headed, black-headed, and rare yellow-headed.
Purple Martins are completely dependent on human-made housing in eastern North America.
The Wrybill is the only bird with a bill that curves to one side, which it uses to probe under stones for insects.
Mourning Doves can drink water by sucking it up like a straw, unlike most birds that scoop and tilt.
The Azure-winged Magpie can use tools and has been observed using sticks to obtain food.
Eastern Bluebirds pair bonds can last multiple breeding seasons, with pairs often reuniting each spring.
The Greater Sooty Owl has the deepest voice of any Australian bird, with calls resembling a bomb dropping.
American Goldfinches are the only finch that molts twice a year, changing from bright yellow to olive-brown.
The Mute Swan is one of the heaviest flying birds, with males weighing up to 30 pounds.
Killdeer perform a 'broken wing display' to lure predators away from their nests.
The Fork-tailed Drongo can mimic the alarm calls of other species to scare them away from food.
Great Grey Owls can detect prey under 2 feet of snow and break through crusty snow with their talons.
The Helmeted Guineafowl's distinctive call sounds like a rusty gate opening.
White Pelicans hunt cooperatively, forming a line and herding fish into shallow water.
The Red-tailed Hawk's screech is the sound effect used for Bald Eagles in movies—eagles actually have a much weaker call.
Whooping Cranes stand 5 feet tall and have a wingspan of 7.5 feet, making them North America's tallest bird.
The Atlantic Puffin can hold an average of 10 fish in its beak at once, arranged neatly in a row.
Sanderlings run back and forth at the edge of waves on beaches, feeding on small invertebrates.
The Greater Yellowlegs gets its name from its distinctive bright yellow legs.
European Robins were one of the first birds proven to use Earth's magnetic field for navigation.
The Snail Kite has a specialized curved bill perfectly shaped for extracting apple snails from their shells.
Common Ravens can live up to 21 years in the wild and have been recorded living over 40 years in captivity.
The Hoopoe has a crown of feathers that opens like a fan when alarmed or excited.
Laysan Albatrosses can fly 50,000 miles per year searching for food to bring back to their chicks.
The American Dipper can walk on the bottom of fast-flowing streams by angling its body to use the current as downforce.
Scarlet Ibis get their brilliant red color from the carotene in the crustaceans they eat.
The Common Nighthawk catches insects on the wing and can consume hundreds in a single night.
Red Kites were once so common in London they were mentioned by Shakespeare as cleaning the streets.
The Ivory Gull is the only all-white gull species and lives in the high Arctic year-round.
Great Egrets were nearly hunted to extinction for their plumes, which led to the founding of the Audubon Society.
The Tawny Frogmouth is often mistaken for an owl but is actually related to nightjars.
Common Murres nest on cliff ledges in colonies so dense that birds are practically touching.
The Indian Roller performs spectacular aerial acrobatics during courtship, tumbling through the sky.
Black-necked Stilts have the second-longest legs relative to body size of any bird.
The Ruddy Duck has a bright blue bill during breeding season that turns grey in winter.
Common Loons need at least a quarter-mile of water for takeoff because of their heavy bodies and small wings.
The White-breasted Nuthatch is the only bird in North America that regularly walks down tree trunks headfirst.
Yellow-billed Oxpeckers remove ticks and parasites from large mammals like rhinos and buffalo.
The Common Cuckoo is a brood parasite that lays its eggs in other birds' nests.
Northern Gannets dive from heights of up to 130 feet at speeds of 60 mph to catch fish.
The Scaled Quail has distinctive white-tipped crest feathers that look like cotton.
Roseate Spoonbills swing their specialized bills side to side through shallow water to catch prey.
The House Sparrow was introduced to North America in 1851 and is now one of the most widespread birds.
Eurasian Oystercatchers use their strong bills to pry open shellfish and can consume 400 cockles per day.
The Belted Kingfisher digs burrows up to 8 feet long in riverbanks for nesting.
Cedar Waxwings pass berries down a line of birds sitting on a branch in an unusual courtship behavior.
The Grey Heron can stand motionless for over 30 minutes waiting for fish to swim within striking range.
Chestnut-backed Chickadees can remember the location of thousands of seed caches for up to a month.
The Black-necked Grebe performs an elaborate mutual penguin dance during courtship.
Red-breasted Nuthatches smear tree sap around their nest entrance, possibly to deter predators.
The Egyptian Plover has a symbiotic relationship with crocodiles, picking food from between their teeth.
Green Herons are one of the few birds known to use tools, dropping bait like insects onto water to attract fish.
The Resplendent Quetzal's tail feathers can grow up to 3 feet long in males.
Common Grackles have iridescent plumage that can appear purple, bronze, or green depending on the light.
The Yellow-throated Warbler is one of the earliest spring migrants, returning to breeding grounds in February.
Snow Buntings breed further north than any other passerine bird, nesting in the high Arctic.
The Guianan Cock-of-the-rock performs spectacular lek displays where males compete for female attention.
Pileated Woodpeckers excavate rectangular holes in trees large enough to weaken or kill the tree.
The American Avocet has a distinctive upturned bill that it sweeps through water to catch small invertebrates.
Long-eared Owls can make themselves look thin and tall like a branch when threatened.
The Blue-footed Booby's foot color is an indicator of health—brighter blue means better nutrition.
Calliope Hummingbirds are the smallest breeding bird in the United States, weighing only one-tenth of an ounce.
The Hooded Oriole uses palm fibers to weave its hanging nest.
American White Pelicans work together in groups to herd fish into shallow water for easier catching.
The Greater Painted-snipe exhibits reverse sexual dimorphism—females are larger and more colorful than males.
Western Grebes rush across water together during courtship in a behavior called rushing ceremony.
The Brambling migrates from Scandinavia to southern Europe and Asia in massive flocks numbering millions.
Yellow-rumped Warblers can digest the waxes in bayberries, allowing them to winter further north than other warblers.
The New Caledonian Crow can manufacture and use multiple types of tools to obtain food.
Tawny Owls have been known to use the same nesting site for over 20 consecutive years.
The Variegated Fairy-wren is one of the few bird species where helpers assist in raising offspring that aren't their own.
Rock Ptarmigans have feathered feet that act like snowshoes in winter.
The Channel-billed Cuckoo is the world's largest brood parasite, laying eggs in the nests of Australian corvids.
American Kestrels cache prey by impaling it on thorns or wedging it in tree bark crevices.
The Inca Tern has a distinctive white moustache of feathers and nests in burrows, caves, or rocky crevices.
Black-billed Magpies are one of the few non-mammal species to hold 'funerals' for deceased members.
The White Tern lays its single egg on a bare branch with no nest at all.
Sooty Shearwaters migrate in a figure-eight pattern across the Pacific Ocean, covering 40,000 miles annually.
The King Penguin's egg incubation period is 54 days, one of the longest of any bird.
Wilson's Storm-petrels are the most abundant seabird species in the world.
The Jabiru stork is the tallest flying bird in South and Central America, standing up to 5 feet tall.
European Goldfinches were a favorite cage bird in Victorian times, leading to significant population declines.
The Blue-gray Gnatcatcher builds its tiny nest using spider silk to bind materials together.
Marbled Murrelets nest in old-growth forest trees, sometimes 50 miles from the ocean.
The Greater Racket-tailed Drongo has tail feathers with bare shafts and twisted tips that produce sound in flight.
Chimney Swifts roost by clinging to vertical surfaces in groups that can number in the thousands.
The Red-billed Tropicbird has elongated central tail streamers that can be twice the length of its body.
Horned Larks are one of the few songbirds native to both North America and Eurasia.
The Dusky Grouse inflates yellow air sacs on its neck during courtship displays.
Common Terns are sometimes called 'sea swallows' due to their graceful flight and forked tails.
The Grey-headed Albatross circumnavigates Antarctica, riding the winds of the Southern Ocean.
Vermilion Flycatchers are one of the most strikingly colored flycatcher species.
The Satin Bowerbird prefers blue objects for decorating its bower and will steal them from nearby bowers.
Black Terns perform elaborate courtship flights, spiraling upward together.
The Crested Caracara is Florida's only native breeding bird of prey that's not a hawk, eagle, or owl.
Sandwich Terns dive from heights of 30 feet to catch fish just below the water's surface.
The Violet-crowned Hummingbird is the only hummingbird with a truly purple crown.
Common Yellowthroats sing a distinctive 'witchity-witchity-witchity' song from dense wetland vegetation.
The Wilson's Phalarope is unusual among shorebirds—females are more colorful and males incubate eggs.
Least Terns are the smallest tern species in North America, weighing less than 2 ounces.
The Green Jay is one of the most colorful members of the corvid family.
Franklin's Gulls migrate from the Canadian prairies to the west coast of South America.
The Magnificent Hummingbird is one of the largest hummingbird species north of Mexico.
Northern Wheatears migrate from Alaska to sub-Saharan Africa, crossing vast stretches of ocean.
The Black Oystercatcher uses its bright orange bill to pry limpets off rocks.
Prothonotary Warblers are the only eastern warbler that nests in tree cavities.
The Ferruginous Hawk is the largest hawk in North America.
Buff-breasted Sandpipers perform courtship displays on Arctic tundra leks.
The Mexican Jay lives in social groups where multiple adults help raise the young.
Piping Plovers nest on sandy beaches and their populations are threatened by human disturbance.
The Groove-billed Ani lives in communal groups where multiple females lay eggs in a single nest.
Cassin's Auklet can regurgitate a stream of oily stomach contents at predators for defense.
The Virginia Rail can compress its body to slip through dense marsh vegetation.
Black-throated Sparrows can survive without drinking water, getting moisture from their food.
The Varied Thrush's song is a single, haunting note that echoes through Pacific Northwest forests.
American Redstarts fan their colorful tails to flush insects from hiding.
The Elegant Trogon excavates nest cavities in sycamore trees along southwestern streams.
Hooded Warblers have a distinctive hood of black feathers framing their yellow face.
The Red Phalarope spins in circles on the water's surface to create upwelling that brings prey to the surface.
White-winged Crossbills have irregular irruptions south when cone crops fail in boreal forests.
The Golden-crowned Kinglet weighs less than a penny but can survive temperatures of -40°F.
Mountain Chickadees cache up to 80,000 seeds each fall and can remember locations for months.
The Tricolored Heron uses a unique hunting technique called 'canopy feeding,' creating shade with its wings.
Grasshopper Sparrows get their name from their insect-like buzzing song.
The Canyon Towhee mates for life and pairs defend their territory year-round.
Le Conte's Sparrows have one of the shortest tails relative to body size of any North American sparrow.
The Hepatic Tanager is named after its liver-red coloration.
Curve-billed Thrashers can run at speeds up to 15 mph across desert ground.
The Yellow-billed Magpie is found only in California's Central Valley and nearby foothills.
Brewer's Sparrows are one of the smallest North American sparrows.
The McCown's Longspur performs a distinctive butterfly-like flight display during courtship.
Allen's Hummingbirds have one of the smallest breeding ranges of any North American hummingbird.
The Pinyon Jay lives in highly social flocks that can number over 500 birds.
Long-billed Curlews have the longest bill of any North American shorebird, up to 8.5 inches.
The California Towhee has a distinctive metallic 'chink' call.
Lark Sparrows have distinctive facial patterns with chestnut and white stripes.
The Costa's Hummingbird can survive in extreme desert heat where temperatures exceed 110°F.
Gray Vireos pump their tails while foraging, unusual behavior for a vireo.
The Lucy's Warbler is the only cavity-nesting warbler in the western United States.
Brandt's Cormorants nest in dense colonies on offshore rocks and islands.
The Phainopepla is the only North American representative of the silky-flycatcher family.
Great-tailed Grackles have expanded their range dramatically northward over the past century.
The Bell's Sparrow is named after naturalist John Graham Bell, who discovered it in California in 1849.
Mountain Plovers nest on barren ground on the Great Plains, preferring areas grazed by prairie dogs.
The Black-chinned Sparrow inhabits chaparral-covered slopes in the southwestern United States.
Lawrence's Goldfinches are nomadic, appearing in different areas from year to year based on seed availability.
